planting.note: Scarify or hot-water-soak seed before sowing, or set out container stock in spring into rocky or caliche, well-drained alkaline soil in full sun; this thorny legume is slow to establish but tough once rooted.

directions: Roemer's catclaw acacia is a multi-stemmed, thicket-forming shrub of the open live oak-juniper savanna and limestone outcrops of the Edwards Plateau and South Texas, where paired recurved thorns along each stem give the plant its common name and its best defense against browsing deer. Rounded clusters of small cream-white, faintly sweet-scented flowers appear in spring and again after summer rain, drawing in a wide range of native bees and butterflies, and are followed by flattened woody seed pods that persist into winter. Plant it in full sun on rocky, shallow, alkaline soil exactly like the thin caliche of its home range; it resents heavy, moisture-retentive ground and needs no irrigation once its taproot is established. Its dense, spiny habit makes it a useful wildlife thicket or barrier planting at the sunny edge of a savanna-style native garden.

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before direct sowing after the last frost into lean, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; established plants resprout from the base each spring.

directions: Twoleaf senna is a low, woody-based perennial of the open limestone savannas and rocky flats of the Edwards Plateau, named for its unusual leaves made of just a single pair of broad, blue-green leaflets rather than the many small leaflets typical of most sennas. From spring through fall it bears bright yellow, five-petaled flowers in loose clusters that serve as a principal host plant for cloudless sulphur and sleepy orange butterfly caterpillars, making it a magnet for both pollinators and egg-laying females. It thrives in the same thin, rocky, highly alkaline soils that support little bluestem and live oak mottes, and resents rich garden soil or regular watering. Expect top growth to die back in hard freezes with reliable regrowth from the woody crown the following spring.

planting.note: Scatter seed onto bare, thin, rocky soil or exposed limestone crevices in fall; the tiny succulent germinates with cool-season rains and needs essentially no care, only bare mineral ground and full sun.

directions: Nuttall's stonecrop is a tiny, mat-forming succulent ephemeral that colonizes the thinnest soil pockets on exposed limestone glades and savanna outcrops across the Edwards Plateau, often growing in cracks too shallow for almost anything else to root. Clusters of small, cylindrical, bead-like leaves turn from green to coppery red under the stress of full sun and dry soil, and in spring the plant is topped with small star-shaped, bright yellow flowers held just above the foliage. It germinates with cool-season rains, completes its life cycle before the heat of summer, and reseeds itself reliably where the mineral soil is left undisturbed. Use it in crevice gardens, shallow hypertufa troughs, or thin-soil rock gardens that replicate its glade habitat; it cannot compete in fertile beds or where mulch or leaf litter accumulates.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into lean, rocky, or caliche soil as part of a wildflower mix; seedlings overwinter as a basal rosette and bloom the following spring.

directions: Spreading bladderpod is a low, branching winter annual common on the thin, rocky, and disturbed limestone soils of the Edwards Plateau savanna and adjoining Blackland prairie, where it often carpets roadside caliche cuts and open glade margins with cheerful yellow bloom in early spring. The small, four-petaled flowers are followed by distinctive inflated, globe-shaped seed pods that give the whole bladderpod genus its common name and persist as an ornamental feature after the petals drop. It germinates with fall rains, overwinters as a flattened rosette of gray-green, star-shaped hairy leaves, and finishes its cycle before the onset of summer heat, reseeding freely in undisturbed bare ground. Include it in native wildflower seed mixes sown over thin, alkaline soil where showier perennials have not yet filled in.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out small plugs in spring into sharply drained, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; established plants need no irrigation and bloom intermittently almost year-round in mild winters.

directions: Rose heath is a small, wiry, mat-forming subshrub of open limestone and caliche flats across the Edwards Plateau and Trans-Pecos, forming tight gray-green mounds of needle-like leaves that stay evergreen through mild winters. Tiny, daisy-like white to pale-pink ray flowers with yellow centers appear in flushes nearly any month temperatures stay above freezing, making it one of the most reliably blooming native groundcovers for thin, rocky soil. It thrives in exactly the shallow, sun-baked, alkaline sites where turf and most garden perennials fail, requiring no supplemental water once its woody taproot is established. Use it as a tough, low edging or filler between limestone pavers, in gravel beds, or cascading over dry rock walls.

planting.note: Scarify seed before sowing, or plant container-grown shrubs in spring into rocky, caliche, well-drained alkaline soil in full sun; expect slow establishment the first year followed by a strong flush of growth and bloom after summer rains.

directions: Texas kidneywood is a many-branched, deciduous shrub scattered through open live oak-juniper savanna and limestone outcrops of the Edwards Plateau and the Rio Grande Plains, where its fine, compound leaflets give the whole plant a soft, airy texture. Dense, upright spikes of tiny white flowers with an intense, honey-like fragrance appear repeatedly through the growing season, especially after rain, drawing heavy traffic from native bees, wasps, and a long list of skipper butterflies that use it as a larval host. It is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant on the thin, rocky, alkaline soils typical of Hill Country savanna and declines quickly in wet or poorly drained ground. Plant it as an understory shrub beneath scattered live oaks or as a pollinator-focused specimen at the sunny edge of a xeric native bed.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, shallow limestone soil; plants form a basal rosette over winter and bloom the following summer, so patience through a full season is required.

directions: Quinine weed is a slender, wiry annual or short-lived biennial restricted to the open limestone glades and shallow caliche flats of the Edwards Plateau and adjacent Hill Country, where its tight, rounded clusters of small, intensely pink, star-shaped flowers form a conspicuous pink haze over bare rock in midsummer. The plant's bitter foliage, reminiscent of true quinine-source gentians, gave rise to its common name and to historical folk use as a fever remedy among early settlers. It needs the identical thin, rocky, mineral soil of its native glades and performs poorly if given fertile garden soil, mulch, or competition from taller plants. Sow it onto scraped, bare limestone-based soil in a dedicated glade or rock garden bed to see its showiest summer display.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or set out nursery-grown offsets in spring into rocky, alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun.

directions: Pineapple cactus forms low, solitary to loosely clustered globose stems studded with prominent tubercles among the shallow-soil limestone barrens and open oak-juniper savanna of the Edwards Plateau, often tucked between exposed bedrock and bunchgrass clumps where little competing vegetation can take hold. Large, satiny yellow flowers with a faint reddish throat open around the stem's crown in late spring, followed by green to yellowish fleshy fruit that ripens through summer and is relished by small mammals. Like most Hill Country cacti it demands sharply drained, gritty, alkaline soil and full sun, and standing moisture or rich organic soil will rot it quickly. It is an excellent, true-to-habitat choice for limestone rock gardens and gravel beds meant to mimic the open savanna rather than shaded canyon settings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
